land.text: Normandy, which Geoffrey of Anjou took when 'in January 1144 he advanced into Rouen' (The Anarchy page)

predecessors.note: Cliopatria keeps continental Normandy in its Norman England row until 1146; from 1147 the Angevin Empire row has it.

land.text: Anjou, Maine and Touraine, the lands of Geoffrey of Anjou (Cliopatria 'Angevins' row, 1126-1146)

predecessors.note: Cliopatria ends its Angevins row in 1146 and starts the Angevin Empire in 1147 with those cells added to Normandy; no page opened dates the union.

land.text: Aquitaine, Gascony and Poitou brought by Eleanor's marriage to Henry in 1152, which Cliopatria draws as Kingdom of France in 1139-1151

predecessors.note: Joined 1152, not at the birth; see the ledger. The kingdom-of-france dossier carries the matching 1152 loss. The duchy-of-aquitaine dossier holds no land between its 1137 loss to France and 1204 (Eleanor was duchess in her own right, but the land is drawn as French).

minus.text: the 1202 shape without Brittany (protectorate), Auvergne (French from July 1189) and Berry (lost by 1199)
the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

union.text: the 1206 shape without Gascony: England, the Welsh March and Ireland
the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

land.text: Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine and the other continental lands lost to Philip II in 1204-1206 (Poitou goes to the county of Poitou, Gascony to the duchy of Aquitaine)

successors.note: Normandy and Anjou in 1204 (John page), Touraine in 1204 (Crown lands page); the rest of Cliopatria's 1202-to-1206 loss is dated by the shape only (confidence 1).

land.text: Poitou, conquered by Philip II in 1205

successors.note: 'Poitou was conquered by King Philip II of France in 1205' (County of Poitou page); the county-of-poitou dossier names this empire as its predecessor.

land.text: the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

successors.note: The duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws the Gascon core of Aquitaine from 1204 (its ledger gain from this empire); this dossier stops drawing it in 1204 so that the land is not drawn twice.

minus.text: the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

land.text: the 1206 shape without Gascony: England, the Welsh March and Ireland

successors.note: England, the Welsh March and Ireland, which Cliopatria carries as the Kingdom of England from 1210 (its 1210 shape has the same cells as the 1206 Angevin shape, Gascony included: the Kingdom of England dossier must leave Gascony to the duchy of Aquitaine).

Brittany, occupied by Henry II 1166-1181 and an Angevin protectorate to 1206 on the pages; Cliopatria's Brittany row resumes in 1206 and the duchy-of-brittany dossier draws the duchy itself for 1188-1205.

capitals.name: Rouen
capitals.note: The Anarchy page: 'in January 1144 [Geoffrey] advanced into Rouen, the capital of the duchy'. For 1144-1146 the dossier's land is Normandy alone (Anjou is in Cliopatria's 'Angevins' row).

capitals.name: Angers
capitals.note: The infobox says 'No official capital. Court was generally held at Angers and Chinon.' Chinon (47.17 N, 0.24 E) was the second seat; the pages do not date either. Angers is the seat from 1147, when Anjou joins the shape; the ledger loses Anjou in 1204.

capitals.name: Westminster (London)
capitals.note: After 1204 what is left of the empire is England, Ireland and the Welsh March. The Palace of Westminster page: 'the primary residence of the kings of England until 1512'. The Angevin court was itinerant and no page opened says where John held court in 1204-1209.

rulers.name: Geoffrey Plantagenet (Geoffrey of Anjou)
rulers.title: Duke of Normandy and Count of Anjou
rulers.note: The Anarchy page: Henry 'was declared duke by his father' in 1149; the Angevin Empire page says Geoffrey 'formally invested his son Henry as duke in 1150'. Geoffrey remained count of Anjou until his death in 1151.

rulers.name: Henry II
rulers.note: Duke of Normandy 1149/1150, count of Anjou 1151, duke of Aquitaine by marriage 1152, king of England from 25 October 1154 (infobox: '1154-1189: Henry II').

rulers.name: John
rulers.note: Infobox: '1199-1214: John'; this dossier ends in 1209 where Cliopatria's Angevin row ends.

correction.text: Normandy under Geoffrey of Anjou as duke from 1144 (the 'Angevins' row keeps Anjou, Maine and Touraine until 1146)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's Angevin Empire row starts in 1147, but 'in January 1144 [Geoffrey] advanced into Rouen, the capital of the duchy' and was 'recognised as duke of Normandy after taking Rouen in 1144'. For 1144-1146 Cliopatria draws Normandy inside its Norman England row (to 1146) and Anjou, Maine and Touraine as 'Angevins' (to 1146); this keyframe carries only Normandy so as not to double-draw Anjou.

64,338 km2 for 1147-1151: Normandy (127 of the gazetteer's 129 cells) plus Anjou, Maine and Touraine. The page gives no area (lead: 'roughly all of present-day England, half of France, and parts of Ireland and Wales'), so the infobox comparison is empty. Geoffrey was duke of Normandy from 1144 and count of Anjou until his death; Henry 'inherited his position as count of Anjou' in September (1151, the year inferred). Louis VII's recognition of Henry as duke in August 1151 cost 'concessions in the Norman Vexin' (ledger).

correction.text: the 1152 shape without Auvergne, for 1152-1153 (from October 1154 the keyframe angevin-empire_1154 applies)

keyframe_review.note: 205,827 km2 for 1152-1168: Aquitaine, Gascony, Poitou, Berry, Limousin and Auvergne added to the 1147 core after 'Henry married Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1152, acquiring the Duchy of Aquitaine'. The shape includes Auvergne from 1152, but the page has Henry only marching 'into Auvergne in 1167' (ledger), so Auvergne is removed until then. The shape also leaves out England, which Henry took on 25 October 1154: see the new keyframe angevin-empire_1154, which supersedes this one from 1154. This verdict holds for 1152-1153 only.

correction.text: the Angevin continental lands of 1152 plus England and the Welsh March (Cliopatria's Norman England shape of 1152), without Northumberland and Cumbria (Scottish until 1157) and without Auvergne (not held until 1167)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: 'Henry became King Henry II of England upon Stephen's death on 25 October 1154', so England belongs to the empire from 1154, not from Cliopatria's 1169 (when its Angevin shape first includes England; Cliopatria's Norman England row runs separately 1152-1168). The Scots held Northumberland and Cumbria until 1157 (The Anarchy page), so they are left out until the ledger's 1157 gain, and Auvergne until 1167.

354,971 km2 for 1169-1176 as Cliopatria draws it, but right only for 1169-1170: it is exactly the union of the 1152 Angevin shape and the 1152-1168 Norman England shape (607 of its 608 cells overlap), it has no Irish cell (modern countries France and United Kingdom, western edge 5.77 W), and Henry II took Leinster and Waterford in October 1171 (ledger), so the new keyframe angevin-empire_1171 draws 1171-1176. By 1169 Northumberland and Cumbria are back (1157) and Auvergne is in (1167); 'By 1169, the duchy [of Brittany] was firmly under Angevin control' is drawn as occupied land, not in the shape.

correction.text: the 1169 shape unchanged, for 1169-1170 only; from 1171 the keyframe angevin-empire_1171 applies (the same shape plus Leinster and Waterford)

union.text: Leinster, held in fief by Strongbow, and the crown towns of Dublin, Wexford and Waterford

correction.text: the 1169 shape plus Leinster and Waterford, taken by Henry II in October 1171

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1171-1176: Cliopatria draws no Irish cell before 1177, but 'On 17 October 1171, King Henry landed at Waterford with a large army' and 'declared Dublin, Wexford and Waterford to be crown land', with Strongbow holding Leinster in fief (ledger, 1171). The region is the Leinster entry of the gazetteer plus a 30 km circle round Waterford (83 cells, of which Cliopatria's 1177 shape holds 66). The Treaty of Windsor (6 October 1175) split Ireland into two spheres and moved no drawn land. The lordship-of-ireland dossier (eu-11-x) now draws the same Anglo-Norman land from 1171: the orchestrator must give it to one of the two.

correction.text: the 1177 shape with the Irish cells that Cliopatria adds in 1188 (Munster and east Ulster): de Courcy's Ulster is dated February 1177 and the grants of Thomond and Desmond 1177

keyframe_review.note: 371,770 km2 for 1177-1187: Cliopatria adds Leinster, Meath and Oriel in 1177 (67 cells), and Munster and east Ulster only in 1188. The Anglo-Norman invasion page puts de Courcy in Ulaid in February 1177 (Downpatrick) and the grants of Thomond and Desmond in 1177, with Anglo-Norman invasions of Desmond, Thomond and Connacht 'over the following months'; both are in the ledger for 1177, so the shape adds them from 1177.

correction.text: the 1188 shape without Brittany (occupied 1166-1181, a protectorate after)

keyframe_review.note: 419,597 km2 for 1188-1191: adds Brittany (about 127 cells, because Cliopatria's Duchy of Brittany row has no shape for 1188-1205) and Munster and east Ulster. The page says Brittany, Cornwall, the Welsh princedoms, Toulouse and Scotland 'were not formal parts of the empire': Henry took control of Brittany in 1166 and Geoffrey received the Breton nobles' homage at Rennes by 1169, so Brittany is drawn as a protectorate tint (ledger: occupied 1166-1181, a protectorate 1181-1206) and taken out of the shape. Auvergne stays in until July 1189, when Henry II renounces his claim to it (ledger; the Philip II page), so for 1189-1191 the shape is the 1188 correction without Auvergne.

correction.text: the 1192 shape without Brittany (protectorate) and without Auvergne (French from July 1189)

keyframe_review.note: 423,252 km2 for 1192-1201: same as 1188 plus a few western Irish cells. Without Brittany (protectorate) and without Auvergne, which Henry II gave up in July 1189 (the Philip II page: Henry had to 'renounce his claim to suzerainty over Auvergne'; the Angevin Empire page says only that Richard 'also recognised Auvergne as being in Philip's royal demesne', with no year). Berry stays in as Cliopatria draws it but the page has only claims there ('Henry and Richard pushed further claims over the County of Berry'; Philip took Berry strongholds in 1188; 'lost completely by the time of the accession of John in 1199'): unverified, the loss is dated 1199.

correction.text: the 1202 shape without Brittany (protectorate), Auvergne (French from July 1189) and Berry (lost by 1199), for 1202-1203; from 1204 the keyframes angevin-empire_1204 and _1205 apply

keyframe_review.note: 426,192 km2 for 1202-1205 as Cliopatria draws it, the largest Cliopatria shape; Ireland to 9.3 W. The 1202 Irish additions (11 cells in west Munster and Connacht) match no dated event on the pages: the Anglo-Norman invasion page has de Courcy and Hugh de Lacy invading Connacht 'on behalf of O'Connor in 1200' (an invasion in an ally's cause, not an annexation), and the Lordship of Ireland page, opened in the repair, is silent on Limerick, Cork and Connacht around 1200. Without Brittany, Auvergne and Berry; right for 1202-1203 only, because the ledger takes Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine and Gascony away in 1204 and Poitou in 1205.

minus.text: the 1202 shape without Brittany (protectorate), Auvergne (French from July 1189) and Berry (lost by 1199)

union.text: the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

correction.text: the 1202 shape (without Brittany, Auvergne and Berry) without Normandy, Anjou, Maine and Touraine (lost to Philip II in 1204) and without Gascony (the duchy of Aquitaine from 1204)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1204: 'By August, Philip had taken Normandy and advanced south to occupy Anjou and Poitou as well' (John page); the Crown lands page adds Touraine ('1204: confiscation of the Duchy of Normandy, the Touraine, Anjou, Saintonge'). Maine is not named on either page (confidence 1 in the ledger). Poitou is still drawn: the County of Poitou page dates its conquest to 1205. 'John's only remaining possession on the Continent was now the Duchy of Aquitaine': the Gascon core goes to the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier, which draws it from 1204, so it is not drawn here (the repair removed it from Cliopatria's 1202 and 1206 shapes). Cliopatria keeps all of this land to 1205; the ledger dates the losses to 1204. Left: England, the Welsh March, Ireland and the remaining continental lands (Saintonge, Limousin, Perigord and similar), which the 1206 entry dates by the shape alone.

minus.text: the 1202 shape without Brittany (protectorate), Auvergne (French from July 1189) and Berry (lost by 1199)

union.text: the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

correction.text: as for 1204 and without Poitou (lost in 1205)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1205: the 1204 shape without Poitou, 'conquered by King Philip II of France in 1205 after he declared it a confiscated fief of the crown' (County of Poitou page; the county-of-poitou dossier draws the county from 1205). The remaining continental lands stay one more year (ledger 1206, confidence 1).

213,179 km2 as Cliopatria draws it for 1206-1209 (England, the Welsh March, Ireland and Gascony), about 186,000 km2 without the 115 Gascony and Gironde cells (746 of 861 cells). 'John's only remaining possession on the Continent was now the Duchy of Aquitaine' after Philip took Normandy, Anjou and Poitou in 1204; in 1206 John took the city of Angers and the year's campaigning ended with a truce (paraphrase; the page also refers to 'the truce of 1206-1208'). The duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws the Gascon core from 1204 (its gain from this empire), so it is taken out here. Cliopatria's Kingdom of England shape for 1210 has the same 861 cells as this shape, Gascony included: the dissolve is 1209 only by Cliopatria's row end.

minus.text: the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

correction.text: the 1206 shape without Gascony: England, the Welsh March and Ireland; the Gascon core is the duchy of Aquitaine's from 1204

region.text: Normandy, the duchy of which Rouen was the capital

ledger.note: 1144: Geoffrey of Anjou takes Rouen and becomes duke of Normandy, the beginning of the Angevin dominion. 'In January 1144 he advanced into Rouen, the capital of the duchy' and was 'recognised as duke of Normandy after taking Rouen in 1144'; the Angevin Empire page: 'Rouen surrendered to him in 1144 and he anointed himself duke of Normandy.' Cliopatria's Angevin Empire row starts only in 1147; Wikipedia dates the 'empire' proper from Henry's accession in 1154 (infobox rulers from 1154).

region.text: Anjou, Maine and Touraine, Geoffrey's county, joined to Normandy in the 1147 shape

ledger.note: 1147: Cliopatria joins Anjou, Maine and Touraine to Normandy. Geoffrey's page has him count of Anjou 'by inheritance from 1129' and of Maine to 1151, and 'on 14 January 1144, he crossed the Seine and entered Rouen', duke of Normandy from the summer of 1144, so the union of Anjou and Normandy under one ruler is 1144 (paraphrase); 1147 is the year of Cliopatria's shape (its 'Angevins' row ends in 1146) and is kept so that Anjou is not drawn twice. Touraine is not on the page. The Angevin Empire page is silent on a date for the union.

region.text: the Norman Vexin, conceded by Henry to Louis VII in return for recognition as duke (circle round Gisors)

ledger.note: 1151: Louis VII recognises Henry as duke of Normandy and takes the Norman Vexin. 'Louis VII had recognised Henry as duke of Normandy in August 1151 in exchange for concessions in the Norman Vexin.' The page does not say how much of the Vexin; a 20 km circle round Gisors stands for it.

region.text: Aquitaine, Gascony and Poitou, with Berry and Limousin as Cliopatria draws them, from Eleanor of Aquitaine

ledger.note: 1152: Henry marries Eleanor and becomes duke of Aquitaine, land that Cliopatria draws as French until then. 'Henry married Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1152, acquiring the Duchy of Aquitaine'; 'Thus Henry became duke of Aquitaine and Gascony and count of Poitou.' Cliopatria draws this land as Kingdom of France in 1139-1151 and as Angevin from 1152, and the kingdom-of-france dossier carries the matching 1152 loss; the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier holds no land between its 1137 loss to France and 1204, so Eleanor's inheritance is named in the note, not as counterpart. Auvergne, which the shape includes, is left out until 1167.

region.text: Vernon and Neuf-Marché on the Norman Vexin frontier

ledger.note: 1154: Henry buys back Vernon and Neuf-Marché from Louis VII. 'Henry bought Vernon and Neuf-Marché back from Louis in 1154.' A 15 km circle round Vernon stands for the two places.

region.text: England and the Welsh March of Cliopatria's Norman England shape, without Northumberland and Cumbria

ledger.note: 25 October 1154: Stephen dies and Henry becomes King Henry II of England, joining England to the Angevin lands. 'Henry became King Henry II of England upon Stephen's death on 25 October 1154.' Cliopatria draws England in the Angevin Empire only from 1169; its Norman England row runs to 1168. Northumberland and Cumbria are Scottish until 1157.

region.text: the lands in the north of England returned by Malcolm IV: Northumberland and Cumbria

ledger.note: 1157: the Scots hand back the north of England. 'In 1157 pressure from Henry resulted in Malcolm IV of Scotland returning the lands in the north of England.' The Angevin Empire page: Northumberland was lost 'when Malcolm handed it back in 1157'. The Scots had held Carlisle since 1135-36 and Northumbria by the Treaty of Durham of 1139 (see the norman-england ledger).

region.text: Nantes and its surrounding territories

ledger.note: September 1158: Conan IV surrenders Nantes to Henry II. 'At Michaelmas 1158, Conan IV surrendered Nantes and its surrounding territories to King Henry II at Avranches.' The County of Nantes page lists Henry II as count 1158-1185 and the Henry II page has Henry, when Geoffrey died in 1158, 'annexed it for himself'. Cliopatria's Angevin shapes leave Nantes in the Duchy of Brittany row, so the gain is not in a keyframe.

region.text: Quercy: Cahors and the castles of the Garonne valley

ledger.note: 1159: Henry takes Cahors and Quercy from Toulouse. 'Henry did capture Cahors along with castles in the Garonne valley in the Quercy region'; 'Only Quercy was directly administered by the Angevins after Henry II's conquest in 1159.' Toulouse itself was not taken. The gazetteer has no Quercy; a 40 km circle round Cahors stands for it.

region.text: the Norman Vexin, round Gisors

ledger.note: November 1160: Henry II seizes the Norman Vexin when his son marries Louis VII's daughter Margaret. The page has the 1158 agreement to betroth Henry's eldest living son to Margaret, with Louis granting 'the disputed territory of the Vexin to Margaret on her marriage', and that in November, after the 1160 treaty, Henry 'bullied several papal legates into marrying them' and 'promptly seized the Vexin' (the year is implied by the context). The Angevin Empire page has the betrothal on 2 November 1160. A 20 km circle round Gisors stands for the Norman Vexin, as in the 1151 loss.

region.text: lands along the Brittany-Normandy border

ledger.note: 1164: Henry II seizes lands on the border between Brittany and Normandy. 'In 1164, Henry intervened to seize lands along the border of Brittany and Normandy'; the page names no place, so the Couesnon marches round Mont-Saint-Michel (the circle the duchy-of-brittany dossier also uses) are a reading.

region.text: the whole duchy under Henry II's guardianship

ledger.note: 1166: Henry II forces Conan IV to abdicate and takes the duchy under his guardianship. 'Henry then forced Conan to abdicate as duke and to give Brittany to his heir and daughter Constance'; 'Henry II held guardianship over Brittany for Conan's daughter Constance' until the marriage of 1181. The Angevin Empire page: 'By 1166, it became apparent that Conan was unable to independently maintain order in Brittany' and 'By 1169, the duchy was firmly under Angevin control'; it lists Brittany among areas that 'were not formal parts of the empire', so the duchy is occupied land (hatched), not territory in the shape. Changed from vassal_start to occupation_start to match the duchy-of-brittany ledger (occupation 1166-1181).

region.text: Auvergne, which Henry II entered in 1167

ledger.note: 1167: Henry marches into Auvergne. 'In 1167, Henry II marched into Auvergne'; the page says Auvergne 'was also part of the empire for parts of Henry's and Richard's reigns'. Cliopatria's Angevin shape includes Auvergne from 1152; the page dates nothing there before 1167.

region.text: Leinster, held in fief by Strongbow, and the crown towns of Dublin, Wexford and Waterford

ledger.note: 17 October 1171: Henry II lands at Waterford and takes Dublin, Wexford and Waterford as crown land, with Leinster held of him by Strongbow. 'On 17 October 1171, King Henry landed at Waterford with a large army'; 'He let Strongbow hold Leinster in fief and declared Dublin, Wexford and Waterford to be crown land.' Cliopatria shows no Irish land until 1177.

region.text: the County of Toulouse

ledger.note: 1173: Raymond V of Toulouse pays homage to Henry at Limoges. 'In 1173 in Limoges, Raymond finally gave up after over a decade of constant fights' and paid homage to Henry and to his sons Henry and Richard.

region.text: the Kingdom of Scotland under William the Lion, with English garrisons in Edinburgh, Roxburgh, Jedburgh and Berwick

ledger.note: 1174: William the Lion of Scotland becomes Henry's vassal by the Treaty of Falaise. 'He was captured at the Battle of Alnwick and had to sign the tough Treaty of Falaise'; 'Garrisons were to be set in the castles of Edinburgh, Roxburgh, Jedburgh and Berwick.' The page gives 1174 only in its link titles ('Battle of Alnwick (1174)').

region.text: Ireland outside the Norman-held east and south, which Ruaidri Ua Conchobair held of Henry

ledger.note: 6 October 1175: the Treaty of Windsor makes Ruaidri Ua Conchobair Henry's vassal over the rest of Ireland. 'The treaty divided Ireland into two spheres of influence': Henry overlord of the Norman-held land, Ruaidri overlord of the rest, including Connacht, and Ruaidri swore fealty to Henry (paraphrase). The region is the island outside the Norman-held land of Cliopatria's 1188 shape.

region.text: east Ulster (Down and Antrim), Ulaid, taken by John de Courcy from Downpatrick

ledger.note: February 1177: John de Courcy conquers east Ulster. 'In February 1177, John de Courcy left Dublin with a force of about 22 knights and 500 soldiers'; he took Downpatrick and pushed into Ulaid (paraphrase). Cliopatria draws the east Ulster cells only from 1188.

region.text: Ireland outside the Norman-held east and south

ledger.note: May 1177: Henry makes his son John Lord of Ireland and the Treaty of Windsor lapses in practice. 'Henry declared his son John (aged ten) to be Lord of Ireland', meaning John to become king of all Ireland; 'over the following months' the Anglo-Normans invaded Desmond, Thomond and Connacht. The page does not say the treaty was repudiated.

region.text: Munster: the kingdoms of Desmond and Thomond, granted to FitzStephen, de Cogan and de Braose

ledger.note: 1177: the kingdoms of Thomond and Desmond are granted to Anglo-Normans. 'He granted the kingdom of Thomond to Philip de Braose', Desmond going to Robert FitzStephen and Miles de Cogan; the Anglo-Normans invaded Desmond, Thomond and Connacht 'over the following months'. The page does not say how much was held; Cliopatria's Munster cells (Cork, Limerick, Kerry) appear in 1188 and are brought forward to 1177.

region.text: the whole duchy returns to its duchess and her husband Geoffrey

ledger.note: 1181: Henry's son Geoffrey becomes duke of Brittany and the guardianship ends. 'Geoffrey became Duke of Brittany in 1181' (this page); the Conan IV page has Richmond and Nantes 'held by Henry himself until 1183, and 1185/1186, respectively', 'following the marriage in 1181'. Nantes stays Angevin to 1185 (ledger).

region.text: the Duchy of Brittany (Cliopatria shape of 1169-1187)

ledger.note: 1181: Brittany under Henry II's son Geoffrey is a protectorate of the empire. The page lists Brittany among the areas where the Plantagenets held varying control (paraphrase) that 'were not formal parts of the empire'; the Treaty of Le Goulet page (May 1200) has John pay 'Philip 20,000 marks as relief in exchange for formal recognition of his rule over Brittany'. The year is the page's, the reading as a protectorate is mine. The duchy-of-brittany dossier has no matching relation for 1181-1205 (it draws the duchy as its own state, new keyframe 1188-1205): a mirror is missing there.

region.text: Cahors, retaken by Raymond V of Toulouse

ledger.note: 1183: Raymond V of Toulouse retakes Cahors. Paraphrase of the Angevin Empire page: in 1183 Raymond retook Cahors (the page says Quercy 'did remain a contested area').

region.text: Nantes and its surrounding territories

ledger.note: 1185: Nantes returns to the Duchy of Brittany. The County of Nantes page lists Henry II as count 1158-1185, then 'Geoffrey II, Henry II's fourth son, married to Conan's daughter Constance' (1185-1186) and Constance (1185-1201), and says the county 'was merged permanently into the Ducal crown of Brittany'; the Conan IV page has Henry holding Nantes until '1185/1186'.

region.text: the County of Toulouse

ledger.note: 1188: Raymond V attacks again, joined by the Lusignans, ending his homage. Paraphrase of the Angevin Empire page: in 1188 Raymond attacked again, joined by the Lusignans; the 1190s attack was repelled with help from Navarre.

region.text: Auvergne, recognised as part of Philip II's royal demesne

ledger.note: July 1189: Henry II gives up his claim to Auvergne to Philip II. The Philip II page has Henry having to 'renounce his claim to suzerainty over Auvergne' in July 1189 (4 July, with Issoudun and Graçay confirmed to Philip). The Angevin Empire page says Richard 'also recognised Auvergne as being in Philip's royal demesne' and gives no year (the sentence follows the account of his coronation in November 1189); the Richard I page and the Treaty of Louviers page (January 1196) do not mention Auvergne. The earlier version of this entry wrongly said that 1189 is the Angevin Empire page's year: year and month are the Philip II page's; that all of Auvergne, as Cliopatria draws it, is meant is my reading.

region.text: the Kingdom of Scotland

ledger.note: 5 December 1189: Richard I annuls the Treaty of Falaise and Scotland is free again. 'On 5 December 1189, Richard I annulled the treaty'; he returned Roxburgh and Berwick and acknowledged Scotland's independence.

region.text: the Norman Vexin, round Gisors

ledger.note: 1193: Philip II takes Gisors and the Norman Vexin while Richard I is a captive. 'The fall of the Château de Gisors to the French in 1193 opened a gap in the Norman defences', and Philip's conquests included 'a part of Normandy called Norman Vexin facing French Vexin'. The Philip II page has Gisors surrendering 'without putting up a struggle' in early 1193; the Angevin Empire page has the deal that would give Philip 'the Vexin and the castle of Gisors' in January 1193. The Treaty of Le Goulet (1200) later confirms the cession.

region.text: the County of Berry

ledger.note: By John's accession in 1199 Berry is lost. 'The county was lost completely by the time of the accession of John in 1199'; Philip took Berry strongholds in 1188. The page says Henry and Richard only 'pushed further claims' there, so how much was ever held is unclear. The Treaty of Le Goulet page (May 1200) has John give up 'Évreux, Issoudun, Graçay, and other lands in Berry', and the royal-domain-of-france dossier dates its Berry gain to May 1200: the formal cession follows the de facto loss.

region.text: Évreux (circle; the place is not in the gazetteer)

ledger.note: May 1200: by the Treaty of Le Goulet John gives Philip II the county of Évreux. 'The Treaty of Le Goulet was a treaty signed by Kings John of England and Philip II of France in May 1200'; John 'gave up the Vexin (except for Les Andelys, where the important fortress of Château Gaillard stood)' and gave up 'Évreux, Issoudun, Graçay, and other lands in Berry'. Philip had 'captured and sacked' Évreux in 1198 (Philip II page); the Crown lands page has the County of Évreux and Issoudun annexed in 1200 'in exchange for the king's recognition of John of England' and the kingdom-of-france dossier dates its Eure gain 1200. The Vexin is the 1193 entry, Berry the 1199 entry.

region.text: Normandy, invaded by Philip II

ledger.note: 1202: Philip II invades Normandy. 'In 1202, Philip II launched an invasion of Normandy that culminated in the six-month Siege of Chateau Gaillard, which led to the conquest of the duchy and of neighbouring territories'; the John page: Philip declared John in breach of his feudal duties and 'began a new war'.

region.text: Normandy

ledger.note: 1204: Normandy falls to Philip II. 'In March 1204, Gaillard fell'; 'By August, Philip had taken Normandy and advanced south to occupy Anjou and Poitou as well' (the year is implied by the sequence). Normandy stayed a distinct French fief; the Treaty of Paris of 1259 is outside this page.

region.text: Normandy

ledger.note: 1204: the fighting for Normandy ends with Philip's conquest. 'By August, Philip had taken Normandy.'

region.text: Anjou

ledger.note: 1204: Anjou is occupied by Philip II. Philip 'advanced south to occupy Anjou and Poitou as well' (by August). In 1206 John took Angers, but the year's campaigning ended with a truce (paraphrase). Poitou, named in the same sentence, is the 1205 entry below because the County of Poitou page dates its conquest to 1205.

region.text: Touraine

ledger.note: 1204: Touraine is confiscated from John. The Crown lands page: '1204: confiscation of the Duchy of Normandy, the Touraine, Anjou, Saintonge and, temporarily, of the Poitou' (the entry continues 'from John of England'). The John page does not name Touraine; the region is the gazetteer's.

region.text: Maine

ledger.note: 1204: Maine passes to Philip with Anjou and Touraine (bridging). Neither the John page nor the Crown lands page names Maine, and the county-of-maine dossier has no 1204 event; the Angevin Empire page lists Maine among the empire's counties, and the year follows the same campaign.

region.text: the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

ledger.note: 1204: the Gascon core of Aquitaine, John's only continental holding, becomes the duchy of Aquitaine's own. 'John's only remaining possession on the Continent was now the Duchy of Aquitaine.' The duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws the Gascon core (this region) from 1204 and names this empire as the loser, so the empire stops drawing it here; in 1206 John 'was forced to divert south to counter the invasion of Gascony'. Cliopatria's 1206 shape and its Kingdom of England 1210 shape still contain the land.

region.text: Poitou

ledger.note: 1205: Poitou is conquered by Philip II. 'Poitou was conquered by King Philip II of France in 1205 after he declared it a confiscated fief of the crown'; infobox: 'In personal union with the Kingdom of England; (1154-1205)'. The John page has Philip occupying Anjou and Poitou by August 1204, and the Crown lands page lists Poitou as temporarily confiscated in 1204; the county-of-poitou dossier founds the county in 1205 from this empire.

region.text: the Duchy of Brittany (Cliopatria shape of 1169-1187)

ledger.note: 1206: Brittany leaves the Angevin protectorate (begun in 1181 after the occupation of 1166-1181). The John page says only that 'Brittany rose in revolt' after desertions, without a year; the year is that of Cliopatria's Duchy of Brittany shape (1206-1219) that returns after 1188-1205.

minus.text: the 1202 shape without Brittany (protectorate), Auvergne (French from July 1189) and Berry (lost by 1199)

union.text: the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

minus.text: as for 1204 and without Poitou (lost in 1205)

region.text: the continental lands north and east of Gascony that Cliopatria's shape drops in 1206 (Saintonge, Limousin, Perigord and similar) after Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine and Poitou had gone

ledger.note: 1206: the last continental lands north and east of Gascony are gone. 'John's only remaining possession on the Continent was now the Duchy of Aquitaine'; the page dates no loss beyond Normandy, Anjou and Poitou, so this is the part of Cliopatria's 1202-to-1206 reduction that no earlier entry covers (Saintonge, Limousin, Perigord and similar), dated by the shape. The county-of-perigord and county-of-armagnac dossiers begin in 1206 with no counterpart named; the John page has John in 1206 diverted to Gascony, taking Angers, and a two-year truce.

minus.text: the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

region.text: what remained in 1206-1209: England, the Welsh March and Ireland (Gascony being the duchy of Aquitaine's)

ledger.note: 1209: the last year of Cliopatria's Angevin row; from 1210 the same land (England, Ireland, Gascony) is the Kingdom of England. The pages do not date a dissolution: the empire's continental core was lost in 1204-1206, the infobox rulers run to John in 1214 and the page ends the story with the Truce of Chinon of 28 September 1214. The Battle of Bouvines page says the 1214 victory 'confirmed the collapse of the Angevin Empire' and 'ended all hope of a restoration of the Angevin Empire', and that John 'obtained a five-year truce' (the Truce of Chinon, dated only in its infobox): the year of the end is a convention of Cliopatria's row.

wars.name: Henry II's Toulouse campaign
wars.outcome: Henry gathered his army at Poitiers in June 1159, could not take Toulouse itself but took Cahors and the Garonne castles of Quercy; Raymond V 'finally gave up' and paid homage at Limoges in 1173, retook Cahors in 1183 and attacked again in 1188.

wars.name: Henry II's Welsh expeditions
wars.outcome: 'Henry attacked Wales three times, in 1157, 1158 and 1163', then 'undertook a fourth invasion in 1164, this time with a massive army'; the page says Wales 'obtained good terms provided it paid homage to the Plantagenets' and 'remained almost self-ruling'.
wars.note: No border moved on the pages opened; the 1163 homage of 'the two most powerful princes of Wales' is on the Norman invasion of Wales page and is for the Gwynedd and Deheubarth dossiers.

wars.name: Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland
wars.outcome: The barons landed at Bannow Bay on 1 May 1169, Dublin and Waterford fell in 1170, Henry II landed at Waterford on 17 October 1171 and took Dublin, Wexford and Waterford as crown land; the Treaty of Windsor (6 October 1175) split Ireland into two spheres; John became Lord of Ireland in May 1177.

wars.name: Revolt of 1173-1174 and the Scottish war
wars.outcome: William the Lion was captured at Alnwick (1174) and signed the Treaty of Falaise, placing English garrisons in Edinburgh, Roxburgh, Jedburgh and Berwick; Richard I annulled the treaty on 5 December 1189.
wars.note: The page dates the war only through its link titles.

wars.name: Capetian-Angevin wars of Richard I's reign
wars.outcome: Philip II took Berry strongholds in 1188; Henry II renounced his claim to suzerainty over Auvergne in July 1189 (Philip II page; the Angevin Empire page has Richard recognising it as Philip's demesne without a year); Philip demanded the Vexin in January 1192 and, with John promised the Vexin and Gisors, took Gisors and Neaufles in April-May 1193 (the Richard I page: the fall of Gisors in 1193); the Treaty of Mantes (July 1193) handed John back his estates; Berry was 'lost completely' by 1199.
wars.note: The Treaty of Louviers (December 1195 on the Richard I page, January 1196 on its own page) and the Treaty of Le Goulet (May 1200) are named by pages opened in the repair; Le Goulet's terms are in the ledger.

wars.name: Philip II's conquest of Normandy and the Angevin lands
wars.outcome: Philip summoned John to Paris in 1202, declared him in breach of his feudal duties and invaded; Mirebeau (July 1202) captured the rebels; Chateau Gaillard fell in March 1204; by August Philip held Normandy, Anjou and Poitou; John took Angers in 1206 and a truce followed (1206-1208). John kept only the Duchy of Aquitaine on the Continent.
wars.note: The page names the Treaty of Le Goulet (May 1200) but not its territorial terms; the Anglo-French War page opened second is the 1213-1214 war and was used only for the 1202 invasion sentence.

certainty.note: No treaty line or survey fixes the empire's frontiers on the pages opened: the English-Scottish border (Tweed), the Welsh March, the Irish pale and the frontiers with the French crown are approximate. The Scottish frontier is a treaty line for 1174-1189 only in the sense of the Treaty of Falaise's garrisons.

notes: Pages: 5 of 5 budgeted (plus The Anarchy, shared with the norman-england dossier). (1) Start and end: Cliopatria's row is 1147-1209. The Angevin Empire page gives no dates for the empire itself (infobox rulers 1154-1214); this dossier starts in January 1144, when The Anarchy page has Geoffrey of Anjou take Rouen and the ducal title, and ends in 1209 only because Cliopatria's row ends there and its 1210 Kingdom of England shape has the same cells as the 1206 Angevin shape: the continental lands were lost in 1204-1206 and the pages date no dissolution (confidence-1 event). (2) England: Cliopatria adds England to the Angevin shape only in 1169 and keeps a separate Norman England row to 1168; the page has Henry II king from 25 October 1154, so the keyframe angevin-empire_1154 and the 1154 gain move England here and the norman-england dossier ends in 1154. (3) Brittany: Cliopatria has no Brittany shape for 1188-1205 and folds it into the Angevin shape; the page says Brittany was not a formal part of the empire, so it is drawn as a protectorate (vassal_start 1166, vassal_end 1206) and taken out of the shape; the Brittany dossier (eu-10) must draw Brittany's own land for 1188-1205 or the vassal tint will cover empty ground. (4) Ireland: the page title is 'Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland'; Cliopatria's Ireland grows in 1177, 1188 and 1202; the pages date de Courcy's Ulster to February 1177 and the grants of Thomond and Desmond to 1177, so those are brought forward; the 1202 cells (west Munster, Connacht) are unverified. The Lordship of Ireland (John, 1177) and the Irish provincial kingdoms are for the eu-11-x additions batch. (5) The fetched Angevin Empire text stops in 1193; John's reign comes from the John page. The loss of Maine, Touraine and the remaining north Aquitaine is dated only by the Cliopatria shapes (confidence 1). (6) Not covered by the pages and left out: the 1163 homage of the Welsh princes (named on the Norman invasion of Wales page), Toulouse proper, Cornwall, Scotland beyond 1174-1189; Henry II's Vexin settlement of 1158-1160 and the Treaty of Le Goulet have no territorial terms on the pages. (7) Region names the gazetteer lacks: Quercy, Norman Vexin (circles used). Failed pages: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-French_War_(1202–1204), its percent-encoded form and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loss_of_Normandy (url_not_found). Counterparts needing dossiers: Kingdom of Leinster, Kingdom of Ulaid, Kingdom of Desmond and Thomond, Ruaidri Ua Conchobair's Connacht, Lordship of Ireland (eu-11-x). REPAIR of 2026-10-25 (batch eu-11-i-fixed, after the review): (a) Auvergne: the loss is now July 1189 at confidence 2 on the Philip II page (Henry II renounces suzerainty, Azay-le-Rideau); the Angevin Empire page leaves Richard's recognition undated, and the earlier claim that 1189 is that page's year was wrong. (b) Gascony: the empire stops drawing the Gascon core in 1204 (ledger loss to duchy-of-aquitaine; keyframes 1204, 1205 and 1206 without it), because duchy-of-aquitaine draws it from 1204; the 1204 and 1205 keyframes also take away Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine and Poitou, as the ledger does. (c) 1152: counterpart kingdom-of-france (the mirror), Eleanor's inheritance in the note; the predecessor link likewise. (d) New keyframe 1171-1176 with Leinster and Waterford; the 1169 shape holds for 1169-1170. (e) Norman Vexin: recovered November 1160 (Henry II page), lost 1193 (Richard I and Philip II pages), Evreux lost May 1200 (Le Goulet). (f) Capitals: Rouen 1144-1146, Angers 1147-1203, Westminster 1204-1209. (g) The 1136-1144 war of Geoffrey's conquest of Normandy is dropped (it lies before 1144 and norman-england carries it). (h) Brittany: Nantes gain 1158 and loss 1185, border lands 1164, occupation 1166-1181 (matching duchy-of-brittany); the protectorate tint is kept for 1181-1206 and has no mirror in duchy-of-brittany. (i) Touraine split from Maine in 1204 (Crown lands page names Touraine; Maine stays at confidence 1); Poitou moved to 1205 with county-of-poitou as counterpart; the 1206 loss now covers only the lands no other entry takes. Not changed: the Irish counterpart strings (Kingdom of Leinster etc.) although lordship-of-ireland, kingdom-of-leinster and others now exist and the Anglo-Norman land is drawn by both this empire and lordship-of-ireland; the orchestrator must choose one owner. Pages opened in the repair: 13 more than the original budget of 5, each for one finding.
